source_evidence.anchor: equation (1.1) and the complex RMS and maximum norm definitions
source_evidence.observation: The exact transform uses the positive-sign, unnormalized convention y(j) = Σ_{k=0}^{N-1} exp(i2πjk/N)x(k), for j = 0,...,N-1, with complex RMS norm ((Σ_k |z(k)|²)/N)^(1/2) and maximum norm max_k |z(k)|. [PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: equation (1.1) and the following norm definitions]

source_evidence.anchor: equations (2.1)-(2.2) and the following variant discussion
source_evidence.observation: The paper writes y = Tx with T(j,k) = exp(i2πjk/N), and factors T into permutation matrices, block Fourier matrices of dimensions N_l, and diagonal twiddle-factor matrices. The factorization applies to both Sande-Tukey and Cooley-Tukey algorithms, with different diagonal matrices D_l. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equations (2.1)-(2.2) and the four remarks following (2.2)]

For floating-point numbers a and b, the arithmetic model is fl(a+b) = a(1+θε)+b(1+θε) and fl(ab) = ab(1+θε), where θ is generic, may differ at each occurrence, and lies in [-1,1]. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equations (3.1)-(3.2) and their following sentence]

source_evidence.anchor: absolute trigonometric model, Theorem 1, and K(N,gamma)
source_evidence.observation: The trigonometric model is fl(sin(fl(a))) = sin(a)+γθε and fl(cos(fl(a))) = cos(a)+γθε, with γ ≥ 0 dependent on the transform-order implementation but independent of input data. Theorem 1 gives the first-order FFT error constant K(N,γ) for N = N_1...N_M. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: absolute sine/cosine model and Theorem 1]

The paper explains that O(ε²) includes all terms of order ε²; it does not provide their coefficients in that explanation. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 760, anchor: sentence immediately preceding equation (3.3)]
The one-dimensional FFT analysis explicitly assumes that the input is exactly representable: fl(x) = x. [PDF p. 5, printed p. 761, anchor: paragraph immediately before equation (3.6)]

The output roundoff-error components are defined by e(j) = fl(y(j)) - y(j), so e is the difference between the computed transform and the exact transform. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: first sentence of the proof of Theorem 1(b)]

source_evidence.anchor: Section 6 discussion of input representation and reverse use of the bounds
source_evidence.observation: The conclusion reiterates that the preceding analysis assumed exactly representable inputs, separately discusses actual input rounding fl(x) = x+δ, and then introduces the different context in which input data is known to fewer significant digits than machine precision and the roundoff bounds are used in reverse. [PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: final two paragraphs of Section 6 on the page]

source_evidence.anchor: prose assertion e = T delta and the two following unnumbered bounds
source_evidence.observation: For the exact complex N-vector output error e, the passage asserts that e = Tδ for some fictional δ and states ||δ||_RMS = ||e||_RMS/√N ≤ εK(N,γ)||x||_RMS + O(ε²) and ||δ||_∞ ≤ ε√N K(N,γ)||x||_RMS + O(ε²). It then gives a qualitative least-significant-digit negligibility criterion. [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: paragraph beginning 'Let the roundoff error be given exactly']

binders: Let N be the order of the one-dimensional complex transform, with indices j,k = 0,...,N-1, and let x ∈ C^N be its input. [PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: equation (1.1)]
Let T ∈ C^{N×N} have entries T(j,k) = exp(i2πjk/N), and let the exact output be y = Tx. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equation (2.1) and the displayed definition of T]
Let N = N_1N_2...N_M describe the FFT factorization used by the inherited Theorem 1 constant K(N,γ). [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1]

Given the computed floating-point FFT output fl(y), define e componentwise by e(j) = fl(y(j)) - y(j); after e is fixed, the selected passage existentially introduces some fictional δ ∈ C^N satisfying e = Tδ. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: proof of Theorem 1(b); PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: assertion e = Tδ]

The error parameters are the computer-dependent ε, generic occurrence-dependent θ ∈ [-1,1], and trigonometric absolute-error constant γ ≥ 0. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equations (3.1)-(3.2); PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: absolute trigonometric model]
hypotheses: The result inherits the assumption fl(x) = x, meaning the input supplied to the analyzed FFT is exactly representable in machine precision. [PDF p. 5, printed p. 761, anchor: assumption immediately before equation (3.6); PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: Section 6 input-representation discussion]

The exact output y = Tx is computed by a floating-point FFT of order N = N_1...N_M under the arithmetic and trigonometric error models used in Theorem 1. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equations (2.1)-(2.2) and (3.1)-(3.2); PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: absolute trigonometric model and Theorem 1]

The inherited constants include the effect of performing the D_l twiddle-factor multiplications separately for l = 1,...,M-1. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: parenthetical paragraph following the radix-2 and radix-4 formulas]
conclusions: There exists a fictional complex N-vector δ such that the output roundoff error is represented exactly as e = Tδ. [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: sentence ending 'e = Tδ for some fictional δ']

Its RMS norm satisfies the exact scaling identity and first-order bound ||δ||_RMS = ||e||_RMS/√N ≤ εK(N,γ)||x||_RMS + O(ε²). [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: first unnumbered bound following e = Tδ]
Its maximum norm satisfies ||δ||_∞ ≤ ε√N K(N,γ)||x||_RMS + O(ε²). [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: second unnumbered bound following e = Tδ]

The paper qualitatively declares the roundoff error negligible if ε√N K(N,γ)||x||_RMS is smaller than the least significant digit of the input data. [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: sentence immediately following the two perturbation bounds]
definitions_and_conventions: The Fourier convention is positive-sign and unnormalized: y(j) = Σ_{k=0}^{N-1} exp(i2πjk/N)x(k). [PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: equation (1.1)]
The matrix form is y = Tx with T(j,k) = exp(i2πjk/N); no 1/√N or 1/N normalization appears in T. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equation (2.1) and the displayed definition of T]

fl(y) denotes the floating-point FFT result, while y denotes the exact transform; e is their exact difference. [PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: paragraph following equation (1.1); PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: proof of Theorem 1(b)]

δ in the selected passage is expressly called fictional: it is an input-space perturbation used to represent output roundoff, not an assertion that the physical input was actually perturbed by δ. [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: phrase 'for some fictional δ']
implicit_context: The selected result is the one-dimensional backward interpretation of the one-dimensional forward-error bound in Theorem 1, not the multidimensional result of Theorem 2. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1; PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: references to a complex N-vector and K(N,γ)]

From y = Tx, e = fl(y)-y, and e = Tδ, it follows algebraically that fl(y) = T(x+δ); this backward-error reformulation is inferred rather than written explicitly in the selected passage. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equation (2.1); PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: definition of e; PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: e = Tδ]

The motivating context is input data whose meaningful precision is lower than machine precision, so the fictional perturbation bound can be compared with the data's least significant meaningful digit. [PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: paragraph beginning 'On the other hand'; PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: least-significant-digit sentence]
statement.algorithm_linkage: The constant is tied to the paper's factorized one-dimensional floating-point FFT for N = N_1...N_M. Equation (2.2) uses permutation matrices P_l, block Fourier matrices B_l, and diagonal twiddle matrices D_l; the factorization covers both Cooley-Tukey and Sande-Tukey variants with different D_l. The displayed K constants count separate D_l multiplications. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equation (2.2) and following variant discussion; PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1 and its parenthetical note]
numerical_model: For floating-point a and b, fl(a+b) = a(1+θε)+b(1+θε) and fl(ab) = ab(1+θε), with a generally different θ at each occurrence and -1 ≤ θ ≤ 1. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equations (3.1)-(3.2) and following sentence]

With radix β, t base-β mantissa digits, and at least t+1 digits used to accumulate sums, ε is 0.5β^(1-t) for rounded operations and β^(1-t) for chopped operations. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: parenthetical definition of ε continuing after equation (3.2)]

If sums are accumulated with only t digits, ε is 0.5(1+1/β)β^(1-t) for rounded operations and (1+1/β)β^(1-t) for chopped operations. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: opening parenthetical paragraph]
Trigonometric evaluation uses an absolute-error model: fl(sin(fl(a))) = sin(a)+γθε and fl(cos(fl(a))) = cos(a)+γθε. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: displayed absolute sine/cosine model]

The constant γ is nonnegative, may depend on how trigonometric functions and their arguments are computed for a given transform order, and is independent of input data. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: sentences surrounding the absolute trigonometric model]
error_notions: e is an exact forward output-error vector, with e(j) = fl(y(j))-y(j). [PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: proof of Theorem 1(b); PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: 'roundoff error be given exactly']
δ is a normwise fictional backward input perturbation whose exact transform equals e. [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: e = Tδ and the two following bounds]

Actual input-representation error is treated separately on printed page 765 through fl(x) = x+δ and an added output-error term; that discussion is not the same assertion as the fictional perturbation on printed page 768. [PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: paragraph beginning 'So far'; PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: phrase 'some fictional δ']
norms: For a complex N-vector z, ||z||_RMS = ((Σ_{k=0}^{N-1}|z(k)|²)/N)^(1/2). [PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: RMS norm definition following equation (1.1)]
For a complex N-vector z, ||z||_∞ = max_{0≤k<N}|z(k)|. [PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: maximum norm definition following equation (1.1)]
For the unnormalized Fourier matrix and the selected δ, the passage states the exact norm relation ||δ||_RMS = ||e||_RMS/√N. [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: first unnumbered perturbation bound]
constants_and_indexing: The transform indices are zero-based: j,k = 0,...,N-1. [PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: equation (1.1); PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: definition of T(j,k)]
For N = N_1...N_M, K(N,γ) = Σ_{l=1}^{M} α(N_l) + (M-1)(3+2γ). [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: definition of K(N,γ) in Theorem 1]
The stage constant is α(N_l)=√2 when N_l=2, α(N_l)=5 when N_l=4, and α(N_l)=2√N_l(N_l+γ) otherwise. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: piecewise definition of α(N_l)]
For radix 2, K(2^M,γ)=(3+√2+2γ)M-(3+2γ); for radix 4, K(4^M,γ)=(8+2γ)M-(3+2γ). [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: parenthetical radix-2 and radix-4 formulas]
In the factorization, P_l is indexed through l=1,...,M+1, B_l through l=1,...,M, and D_l through l=1,...,M-1. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: definitions following equation (2.2)]

The first perturbation bound has no √N multiplying its leading term, whereas the maximum-norm perturbation bound has exactly one factor √N. [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: the two unnumbered bounds]
higher_order_terms: Both perturbation inequalities retain an additive O(ε²) term. [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: the two unnumbered bounds]

Earlier in the derivation, O(ε²) is described only as including all terms of order ε²; no explicit coefficient, sign, uniformity range, or finite-ε threshold is supplied. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 760, anchor: sentence immediately preceding equation (3.3)]
exceptional_values: The cited arithmetic and trigonometric models do not explicitly discuss overflow, underflow, subnormal numbers, NaNs, infinities, or exceptional trigonometric evaluations. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equations (3.1)-(3.2); PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: absolute trigonometric model]

The selected absolute perturbation bounds do not divide by ||x|| or ||y|| and state no explicit nonzero-input hypothesis, although the inherited Theorem 1 is displayed in relative form with ||y||_RMS in its denominator. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1; PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: the two unnumbered bounds]

undebatable_constraints: T must be the unnormalized positive-sign Fourier matrix T(j,k)=exp(i2πjk/N), not a negative-sign or unitary-normalized transform. [PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: equation (1.1); PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: definition of T]
The output error must be e = fl(y)-y for exact y=Tx. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equation (2.1); PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: definition of e(j)]
The passage requires an exact identity e=Tδ for a fictional complex N-vector δ. [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: assertion e = Tδ]
The RMS certificate must preserve both the equality ||δ||_RMS=||e||_RMS/√N and the bound by εK(N,γ)||x||_RMS+O(ε²). [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: first unnumbered bound]
The maximum-norm certificate must be preserved separately and must contain the factor √N: ||δ||_∞≤ε√N K(N,γ)||x||_RMS+O(ε²). [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: second unnumbered bound]
The bound is normwise and uses the RMS norm of x on the right-hand side, even for the maximum-norm bound on δ. [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: both unnumbered bounds]

The inherited analysis assumes fl(x)=x; actual input-rounding error is not included in these two fictional-perturbation certificates. [PDF p. 5, printed p. 761, anchor: assumption before equation (3.6); PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: input-representation discussion]
K(N,γ) must retain its dependence on the factorization N=N_1...N_M, including α(N_l) and the (M-1)(3+2γ) term. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1 definition of K(N,γ)]
The O(ε²) terms may not be silently discarded when reproducing the stated passage. [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: the two unnumbered bounds]

The final least-significant-digit statement is a qualitative conditional conclusion, not an additional exact inequality defining δ. [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: sentence after the two perturbation bounds]

ambiguities.issue: The hidden content of O(ε²) is not quantitatively specified. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 760, anchor: explanation of O(ε²); PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: both perturbation bounds]
ambiguities.evidence: The paper says only that O(ε²) includes terms of order ε² and supplies no coefficient, dependence on N, γ, x, or factorization, sign, uniformity statement, or admissible ε range. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 760, anchor: sentence preceding equation (3.3)]
ambiguities.impact: The displayed result is an asymptotic first-order certificate and cannot, from the cited passage alone, be strengthened into a fully explicit finite-precision inequality with the O(ε²) term removed or assigned a concrete constant. [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: additive O(ε²) in both bounds]

ambiguities.issue: The symbol δ is reused for two conceptually different input perturbations. [PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: fl(x)=x+δ; PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: 'some fictional δ']
ambiguities.evidence: Printed page 765 uses δ for actual input representation error, while printed page 768 explicitly calls δ fictional and defines it through e=Tδ. [PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: input-rounding paragraph; PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: e=Tδ paragraph]
ambiguities.impact: The selected contract must treat δ as the fictional backward perturbation unless actual input rounding is separately introduced; the two meanings must not be conflated. [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: phrase 'fictional δ']

ambiguities.issue: The selected passage does not choose uniquely between Cooley-Tukey and Sande-Tukey FFT variants. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: fourth remark following equation (2.2)]
ambiguities.evidence: The paper says factorization (2.2) holds for both variants, but with different diagonal matrices D_l. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: sentence beginning 'And fourth']

[PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: least-significant-digit sentence]
ambiguities.impact: This sentence should remain a qualitative engineering criterion and not be converted into a precise componentwise theorem without additional conventions. [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: least-significant-digit sentence]

contract_plain_english: For the paper's one-dimensional, positive-sign, unnormalized complex Fourier transform y=Tx, computed by the analyzed factorized floating-point FFT from an exactly representable input x, let e=fl(y)-y be the exact output roundoff error. [PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: equation (1.1); PDF p. 5, printed p. 761, anchor: fl(x)=x; PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: definition of e(j)] The passage says there is a fictional complex input perturbation δ whose exact Fourier transform is e, with ||δ||_RMS exactly ||e||_RMS/√N and at most εK(N,γ)||x||_RMS+O(ε²), while ||δ||_∞ is at most ε√N K(N,γ)||x||_RMS+O(ε²). [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: e=Tδ and the two following unnumbered bounds] Here K(N,γ) is the complete Theorem 1 mixed-radix constant, including the arithmetic and trigonometric error model and separate twiddle multiplications. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1 and K(N,γ)] The source finally offers the qualitative judgment that roundoff is negligible when the leading maximum-perturbation quantity is smaller than the input data's least significant digit. [PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: sentence following the two bounds]
